opus-5.5.text:
Well, it really came down to timing and the people. When I was finishing my PhD, I'd been working on machine learning for language, mostly probabilistic models, and around then it was becoming clear that neural networks were starting to work in a way they hadn't before. You could see the results coming out on speech and on images, and it felt like something big was about to happen.

Brain was one of the very few places where you had both the people who really believed in this approach and the compute to actually test those ideas at scale. In academia you'd have a great idea, but you'd be limited by what you could train on a handful of machines. At Brain, the question became less "can we afford to try this?" and more "is this the right idea?" That was a very exciting shift.

The culture also drew me in. It was small then, very research-driven, very bottom-up. People were encouraged to take on ambitious, somewhat risky projects, and there was a sense that we were figuring things out for the first time. For language in particular, there was a lot of open territory. Applying neural networks to text was not yet the obvious thing to do, and I wanted to be part of showing that it could work.

So it was really the combination: an inflection point in the field, great colleagues, and the resources to pursue big questions. It felt like the place where the future of the field was being built, and I didn't want to watch that from the outside.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Google Brain had leading colleagues, compute, and a role in building the field’s future, but does not say Andrew Dai wanted to move to Silicon Valley or regarded it as the center of AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it came down to the people and the timing. When I finished my PhD and was looking around, Google Brain was this small group of researchers who were betting that neural networks, trained at scale on real data, would actually work, at a moment when most of the field still thought that was a bit of a fringe idea. I'd been doing machine learning research in Edinburgh, mostly on more classical probabilistic models, and I could see that the thing holding a lot of my work back was data and compute. Google had both in abundance.

The other piece was that Brain sat inside a company where the research could actually touch products. I didn't want to spend years writing papers that got cited a handful of times and then disappeared. At Google, if an idea worked, you could put it in front of hundreds of millions of people fairly quickly, and that feedback loop is incredibly motivating. So it was a combination of ambitious people, unusual resources, and a direct path from research to impact. That combination was pretty rare at the time, and I didn't want to miss it.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains why he joined Google Brain, citing its people, resources, and product impact. It does not say he wanted to move to Silicon Valley or regarded it as the center of AI.

sol-6.1.text: What really appealed to me was the opportunity to work on deep learning with people who were thinking about some very fundamental questions. How do we get models to learn from data without needing so much human supervision? How do we make those models useful? Google Brain offered a combination of research freedom, computational resources, and the possibility of putting research into products that people actually use. That combination was very exciting to me.
